chapter_theme: Opens the garden sport after the plants' wedding: the groves are dressed, the queens marry the parijata to the Kama creeper, the king hides by art among his women with Madhavan, and the women, sent out by the chief queen, play in leaves and flowers, paint his portrait, sing his fame and complain of their delicacy, until they reach the artificial hill, where guards post watch and the echo mocks them.

cast.role: Tivittan, the dark gem-hued lord, the king
the king's wives, the sixteen thousand kings' daughters
the brahmin jester Madhavan, the king's companion
the grove, given speech and acts in 1644 and 1645
the chamberlains and old guards who search and guard the grove
the artificial hill, whose echo answers in 1649-1650

1627.reading: The grove is made ready: fountains pour from engines like waterfalls, golden frames stand about, every green grove is given a king's crown, and jewels are hung on each tender-leaved branch.
1627.nuance: The verse crowns the groves as kings (line 3), so the garden is made a court before the women of the king's court take it in 1643. The second line is hard to construe: கந்தனெத் may stand for a post-like shape, and the sense of கனகசாலங்கள் (golden frames or halls) is not fixed.
1627.event: Unnamed workers dress the garden with fountains, golden frames and jewels for the festival.

1628.reading: The king's queens dress the young creeper Kama in bridal finery, join her to the tree, and grow glad, for who would not call the wealth of sweet-smiling sons sweet?
1628.nuance: The tree was called a son raised by the women's hands (1563), so the closing question turns the wedding of two plants into a parent's joy in a child; the verse does not say the joy rests on the child's merit.
1628.event: The queens finish the wedding of the parijata and the Kamavalli creeper and rejoice.

claims.claim: the wealth of sweet-smiling sons is sweet to everyone

1629.reading: While the women enjoy the grove in its flowering season, with love thick in their minds and in the dark-hued lord's, and Kama at his side, the lord hides himself by a stratagem.
1629.event: Tivittan hides by a ruse while the queens enjoy the grove.

1630.reading: Having kept the women playing in the grove, the king's son hides himself by an art that makes the dark a curtain, and he and Madhavan are then close beside the women.
1630.nuance: The verse does not say who sent the women to play; 1631 shows the chief queen sending others, so the hiding and the queen's answer are two halves of one game.
1630.event: Using a magic art that makes darkness a screen, Tivittan and Madhavan hide near the women.

1631.reading: Guessing that the king has hidden, the great queen sends the other golden-vine women to play in the grove, and they dress as girls with bright jewels, sweet smiles and lisping speech.
1631.event: The chief queen, guessing Tivittan is hidden, sends more women to play and they act like children.

1632.reading: Wearing gold girdles and skirts of leaves, with sprouts bound on the breasts and tender shoots at the ears, the women delight the eyes of the lord of the trembling elephant.
1632.nuance: The dress is made of the grove itself, so the women become part of what they play in; the king who is looking is the one who hid in 1629-1630.
1632.event: The women dress in leaves and gold to please the king's eyes.

1633.reading: Some set tender leaves and flowers in their hair, some pluck sprouts while their anklets ring, some hold chowries of flowers with bees beside them, and some hush a flower doll like a child.
1633.event: Women play at dressing and at nursing flower dolls in the grove.

1634.reading: Some make dolls, beasts, birds and faces out of flowers, with petals laid as if painters had drawn them, so that the queens marvel, and then bind these into their hair.
1634.event: Women weave flower figures and garlands so fine that the queens marvel.

1635.reading: Bathed in sandal of the southern hill, bees hovering, hair trailing behind and ear-pendants flashing like rainbows, some play makara lutes and sing the king's rich fame.
1635.nuance: They sing his fame while he is hidden among them, so the praise is addressed to a man who may be listening.
1635.event: Some women play lutes and sing the king's fame.

1636.reading: Some, carrying leaves and flowers in their laps, wait for the lotus-goddess-like queen to be in the mood to be seen; others, longing for the wedding of the flower doll, bend like shoots and sway in the kuravai dance.
1636.event: Women bring flower gifts to the chief queen and join in the kuravai dance.

1637.reading: Some paint the gem-hued lord on a board and draw themselves beside him in a lovers' sulk, drawing sure lines with a fine brush and softening his crown and ear-rings.
1637.nuance: The sulk is painted, not spoken: the women set the quarrel of love in a picture for a man who is hiding nearby.
1637.event: Women paint Tivittan's portrait and themselves sulking at him.

1638.reading: Some sit on a jewelled stone slab by the mango grove, hair spilling over their bamboo-like shoulders, and look back at the sweet-dripping verse they gather to the ear.
1638.nuance: This is the one verse of the run that makes poetry the play; the sense of the last two lines turns on reading செய்யுள் as the verse they hear or recite.
1638.event: Women sit on a stone slab and enjoy verse.

1639.reading: Some, garlands and hair-ends hanging and veils swaying, sing of the sea-hued lord as they swing to and fro on a golden swing in the bower, like lightning in a cloud.
1639.event: Women sing of Tivittan while swinging.

1640.reading: Some pull the inner curled leaf from a young plantain and scratch with bright nail-tips a lake with birds, herds of fighting deer and loving pairs, then give them to the women beside them.
1640.nuance: The pairs (மிதுனம்) scratched into the leaf echo the portrait of the lovers' sulk in 1637: the women picture couples while waiting for the king.
1640.event: Women scratch pictures into plantain leaves and pass them to each other.

1641.reading: Some, delighted by the peacock's dance, sway with it; some rival the koel; some, with their hair behind, hide their arrow-keen eyes behind a hand as they say something to be taken up.
1641.nuance: The third line is hard to place: whether கண்டு நீர் கொண்மின் is a call to look or to take is not settled by the Tamil.
1641.event: Women imitate the peacock and the koel, and some cover their eyes with a hand.

1642.reading: Some say their fingers reddened gathering pollen, others that dust of petals hurt their soft feet, others that a flower garland bent their slender waists, and so the queens of the flower-shouldered king became.
1642.nuance: The women claim delicacy as a boast, the way a lover praises it; the king who is meant to hear is hidden in the grove.
1642.event: The queens make playful complaints of their delicacy.

1643.reading: The women's waists sway like creepers without touching them, their long glances run like jewel-bees, their feet and hands show like tender shoots, and so they conquer the scented flower-grove.
1643.nuance: 1627 crowned the groves as kings; here the women take the crown by being more garden than the garden.
1643.event: The women's beauty outdoes the grove.

1644.reading: The flowers of the grove, bowing as they catch the women's body-fragrance, say they have no way to repay them and gather in clusters, bending with offerings.
1644.nuance: A speech given to the grove, not to a person; the plants admit a debt and not a claim.
1644.event: The grove's flowers bow to the women and offer themselves.

1645.reading: The ashoka gives the women an ashoka, the red tilaka tree gives them tilaka, as if saying that they would serve those who came; the meaning of the last line, about the grove's knowing, is unclear.
1645.nuance: The verse plays on the tree names as gifts: the ashoka is given as an ashoka and the tilaka as a forehead mark.
1645.event: The ashoka and tilaka trees give the women their own sprigs.

1646.reading: Silver-white boulders wrapped in fresh gold spathes, swaying golden coconuts and bird-filled gold plantains frame the artificial hill with clear gem waterfalls, which the women reach.
1646.event: The women reach the artificial hill.

1647.reading: The chamberlains and old guards search the jewelled caves, long thickets and cloud-sleeping groves, and the sweet-spoken ones then take the watch on every side.
1647.nuance: The verse says nothing of finding anyone; the king has hidden himself by art (1630), so the search and the guard are around the only man the women expect.
1647.event: Chamberlains and guards search the grove and then guard its approaches.

1648.reading: Like peahens spreading through the grove, the dark-cloud-hued lord's beloved women enter the hill-slope grove, jewels rolling and girdles sounding.
1648.event: The women enter the grove on the hill-slope, ornaments sounding.

1649.reading: As the girdles at their waists ring, the hill's own girdle rings back, and as their golden anklets sound, a row of golden anklets answers exactly.
1649.nuance: The answering 'girdle' belongs to the hill (வரை மேகலை); only an echo fits the verse, and 1650 confirms it.
1649.event: The women's girdles and anklets are answered by an echo.

1650.reading: The hill takes the women's jewelled lisping, as it was uttered, and answers it back, mimicking what they do and mocking them, in the fragrant grove of the red-eyed tall one.
1650.nuance: The hill acts as a speaker of its own; the red-eyed tall one is the king of the opening (verse 2). The word அசதியாடின்று (made fun of) is read here as mockery in play.
1650.event: The artificial hill echoes and mocks the women's talk.

links.note: 1561 has the chief queen resolve to see the parijata wed to the Kama creeper; 1628 has the queens dress the bride and join her to the tree.
links.teaches: The queen's wish ends in a ritual the women perform themselves, so the festival is theirs and the king only attends.

links.note: 1628 calls the wealth of sweet-smiling sons sweet to all; Kural 63 says people call children their wealth because their wealth comes through their own deeds.
links.teaches: The poem's child is a tree that has no deeds, so its sweetness comes wholly from rearing, which tests whether the couplet's reason is the only one.

gains.a: The wedding gains a reason for the parents' joy that lies in the child's own deeds, which the plant cannot supply, so only the rearing is left to explain it.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case in which the child is a plant and cannot earn anything, so the joy it names is shown to rest at least partly on the care given.

links.note: 1629 says the lord hides by a stratagem; 1630 shows the stratagem, an art that makes darkness a curtain, with Madhavan beside him.
links.teaches: The hiding is done by a magic art and with a companion, so the king does not slip away but joins the women's game unseen.

links.note: 1630 has the king hidden among the women; 1631 has the chief queen guess it and send more women out to play like children.
links.teaches: The queen answers the hiding by staging the game she thinks he wants to watch, so the women's play is her reply and not only their sport.

links.note: 1632 builds the women's beauty out of gold, leaves and sprouts to delight the king's eyes; Naladiyar 46 asks which part of the fresh-garlanded woman is she, among entrails, fat, blood and bone.
links.teaches: The poem makes the body a thing of ornament and the quatrain takes it apart into its parts, so the two disagree on whether the adorned body is a person to be praised.

gains.a: The adorned women gain a test of what is being praised once the leaves, gold and sprouts are taken off.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a body shown at its most dressed and admired, so its question has an object that actually looks like a woman.

links.note: 1637 has the women paint the king and themselves sulking at him; Kural 1329 has the man wish the woman would go on sulking so that he may go on pleading.
links.teaches: The women fix the sulk in paint, where no pleading can follow, so the picture keeps the lovers' quarrel without its making-up.

gains.a: The portrait gains the reading that a sulk is something the lover wants, which explains why the women paint it for him.
gains.b: The couplet gains a sulk that is drawn, not spoken, which separates the delight of being sulked at from the pleading that follows.

links.note: 1642 has the women say a garland bent their slender waists; Kural 1115 has the man say a woman who wore anicham flowers with their stems has a waist too weak for good drums to sound.
links.teaches: What the couplet gives as a lover's praise of a woman's delicacy the poem gives to the women as their own complaint, so the delicacy becomes something they offer to be noticed.

gains.a: The women's complaints gain a source in the convention of praising a woman's frailty, so they speak in the lover's idiom.
gains.b: The couplet gains women who claim the praised frailty themselves, so the frailty is shown as performance as well as praise.

links.note: 1627 crowns the groves as kings and hangs jewels on every branch; 1643 says the women conquer the flower-grove with their waists, glances and limbs.
links.teaches: The grove made a king in 1627 is taken by the women, so the same grove is first a court and then a thing conquered.

links.note: 1647 has the guards search the caves and thickets and then watch every side; 1630 has the king already hidden among the women by art.
links.teaches: The guard stands around a king who is already inside the place it guards, so the watch protects the game and not the king.

links.note: 1646 sets the artificial hill with gem waterfalls as the place the women reach; 1650 makes the same hill answer them and mock them.
links.teaches: The hill that was scenery becomes a speaker, so the grove ends the run by playing back at the women.

links.note: 1649 has the women's girdles and anklets answered by the hill; 1650 has the hill take their lisping and answer it as mockery.
links.teaches: The echo of metal in 1649 grows into an echo of speech in 1650, which turns the sound from answer into jest.

source_issues: Verses 1627-1634, 1636-1642 and 1631 were printed in eight half-lines and repaired into four lines by the build; read as four. 1631 line 1 had a pulli removed after a vowel sign, and so did 1640 line 7.
1633 lines 3-4 print மரவம்பூம் and குரவம்பூங் with an extra nasal, and 1645 line 4 (குலகறிவோ) is hard to construe; those readings are marked uncertain or hedged.
1644 ends in தாழ்ந்த without a finite verb; read here as a participle completing the sentence.
